meta.name: RightPart demo library
meta.notice: Fictional device and parts for demonstration and training. Not engineering data: do not use these values to build or repair real equipment.

parts.name: Pan head screw M3 × 6, Phillips, stainless
parts.tool: PH1 bit, torque driver at 0.4 N·m

details.function: Holds the main circuit board down on its four standoffs.
details.why: The pan head has a wide, flat bearing face that presses the board evenly. Stainless A2 never rusts on the board. 6 mm passes the nylon washer (0.8 mm) and the board (1.6 mm) and still grips about 7 threads of the standoff.
details.ifWrong: An 8 mm screw bottoms out in the standoff, so the board is not clamped and slowly vibrates loose. The Pozidriv look-alike (100-0232) takes a PZ bit: a PH1 bit cams out of it and chews the head.
details.tips: Start all four screws by hand before tightening any of them, then torque them in a cross pattern.

parts.name: Pan head screw M3 × 6, Pozidriv, zinc plated

details.function: General-purpose screw kept for other products. Not used in the Nova-1.
details.why: Zinc-plated steel is cheaper and fine for parts that stay dry.
details.ifWrong: From arm's length it looks exactly like 100-0231. In the Nova-1 it would rust over time, and a Phillips bit cams out of its Pozidriv recess.

parts.name: Button head screw M3 × 8, hex socket, stainless
parts.tool: 2 mm hex bit, torque driver at 0.6 N·m

details.function: Fixes the front bezel to the six bosses on the front frame.
details.why: The button head is low and rounded: it looks clean on the front of the device and has no edge to catch a glove or a cleaning cloth. 8 mm = 4 mm of bezel plus 4 mm into the 5 mm deep boss, so it clamps fully with 1 mm to spare.
details.ifWrong: The 10 mm screw (100-0234) looks the same but is 2 mm longer: it hits the bottom of the 5 mm boss before its head reaches the bezel. The torque driver still clicks, so it feels right, but the bezel is not clamped: it rattles and the screws work loose in transport.
details.tips: A drop of low-strength threadlocker on the first two threads. Check every head sits flat on the bezel.

parts.name: Button head screw M3 × 10, hex socket, stainless
parts.tool: 2 mm hex bit, torque driver at 0.6 N·m

details.function: Fixes the top cover to the front and rear flanges.
details.why: 10 mm passes the cover (1.5 mm) and the flange (1.5 mm) and fully engages the self-clinching nut, with the tip free below. It uses the same 2 mm key as the bezel screws, so one tool does both.
details.ifWrong: It looks identical to the 8 mm bezel screw (100-0233). Fitted in the bezel it bottoms out in the bosses. Since BOM rev C (change ECO-0142) the bezel takes 8 mm screws only.
details.tips: Keep this bin away from the 8 mm bin, or use a different bin colour.

parts.name: Pan head screw M2.5 × 5, Phillips, stainless

details.function: Holds the display module to the front frame through its four mounting ears.
details.why: The display ears have 2.7 mm holes, made for M2.5. The screw is short so it can never reach the glass.
details.ifWrong: An M3 screw does not fit the ear holes: forcing it cracks the ear. A longer screw can press on the back of the display.

parts.name: Pan head screw M3 × 6, Torx, stainless
parts.tool: T10 bit, torque driver at 0.6 N·m

details.function: Fixes the power supply flanges to the base plate.
details.why: The power supply needs a little more torque than the board. Torx takes it without slipping, and its T10 bit cannot be mixed up with the PH1 bit used on the board.
details.ifWrong: A Phillips screw slips at 0.6 N·m and the head gets damaged. A screw longer than 6 mm sticks out under the base plate and the device rocks on the table.

parts.name: Pan head screw M3 × 25, Phillips, stainless
parts.tool: PH1 bit, torque driver at 0.3 N·m

details.function: Fixes the cooling fan to the rear wall, through the fan frame.
details.why: 25 mm = 2 mm wall + 15 mm fan + 4 mm lock nut + a few threads out. A lock nut only locks when the thread passes all the way through its nylon ring.
details.ifWrong: A 20 mm screw is too short: the thread stops inside the nylon ring, so the nut does not lock and the fan rattles loose. Over-tightening cracks the plastic fan frame, which is why the torque is low.

parts.name: Socket head cap screw M3 × 8, stainless

aliases.note: Same code as on 100-0233: to be checked

details.function: Used on other products where a strong joint is needed. Not used in the Nova-1.
details.why: The tall head takes more torque than a button head.
details.ifWrong: Same thread and length as the bezel screw (100-0233), but the tall head sticks out of the bezel and needs a 2.5 mm key.

parts.name: Pan head screw #4-40 × 1/4, Phillips, zinc plated

details.function: Inch screw kept for a US-made accessory. Not used in the Nova-1.
details.why: Parts designed in the US use unified (inch) threads.
details.ifWrong: It is almost the same size as M3 × 6, but it has 40 threads per inch (0.635 mm pitch) instead of 0.5 mm: it starts in an M3 hole, then jams and strips the thread.

details.function: Plain nut once used on the fan. Retired.
details.why: Replaced by the nylon-insert lock nut 100-0311 because plain nuts shook loose on the fan.

parts.name: Hex nut M4, stainless
parts.tool: 7 mm nut driver, torque driver at 1.2 N·m

details.function: Clamps the protective earth (PE) ring terminal on the earth stud.
details.why: The M4 stud is the earth point of the chassis. Stainless so the contact never corrodes.
details.ifWrong: A loose earth nut is a safety failure: in a fault, the metal case could become live. Never use the earth stud to hold anything else.

parts.name: Lock nut M3, nylon insert, stainless

details.function: Locks the four fan screws so vibration cannot turn them loose.
details.why: The fan vibrates for its whole life. The nylon ring grips the thread and stops the nut turning.
details.ifWrong: A plain nut shakes loose. A lock nut that has been removed once grips less: always fit a new one.

parts.name: Star washer M4, external teeth, stainless

details.function: Two of them sandwich the earth ring terminal on the earth stud.
details.why: The teeth cut through the anodising and lock the nut, so the earth bond stays low-resistance for the life of the device.
details.ifWrong: A plain or split washer does not cut through the coating: the earth bond can fail the safety test, or pass at the factory and fail later in use.

details.function: Sits under each board screw.
details.why: Nylon spreads the load without scratching the board's protective coating, and keeps the screw head off the tracks near the hole.
details.ifWrong: A metal washer (100-0314) can scratch through the solder mask and short a track next to the hole.

details.function: General-purpose washer. Not used in the Nova-1.
details.why: Spreads the load under a screw head on metal parts.

details.function: Kept for older products. Not used in the Nova-1.
details.why: A split spring ring that resists loosening a little.
details.ifWrong: Never a substitute for the star washer on the earth stud: it does not cut through the anodising.

parts.name: Hex standoff M3 × 10, male-female, nickel-plated brass
parts.tool: 5.5 mm nut driver, torque driver at 0.5 N·m

details.function: Holds the main board 10 mm above the base plate.
details.why: 10 mm leaves room for the tall parts under the board and lets air flow. Brass is easy on the thread of the aluminium base.
details.ifWrong: The 12 mm standoff (100-0411) lifts the board 2 mm: the display cable then pulls on its connector.
details.tips: Brass is soft: above 0.6 N·m the male thread can shear off in the base plate.

parts.name: Hex standoff M3 × 12, male-female, nickel-plated brass

details.function: Used on other products. Not used in the Nova-1.
details.why: Gives 12 mm of clearance under a board.

parts.name: Chassis, Nova-1 (base, rear wall, front frame)

spec.fitted: Earth stud M4, IEC power inlet, 12 self-clinching nuts

details.function: The metal frame every other part mounts to, and the earth reference of the device.
details.why: Folded aluminium is light and stiff, and the anodising protects it from cleaning agents.
details.tips: Inspect for dents and scratches before you start. The earth stud must be clean and bare.

details.function: The front face of the device. Frames the display and protects its edge.
details.why: Black anodising does not reflect light into the user's eyes.

details.function: Closes the device and keeps fingers away from the inside.
details.why: One U-shaped part covers the top and both sides.

spec.connectors: J1 power, J3 display, J5 fan

details.function: Runs the device: reads the touch screen, controls the fan and power.
details.why: One board keeps the wiring short.
details.ifWrong: Static discharge from a hand can damage it without any visible sign.
details.tips: Hold it by the edges only, with a grounded wrist strap.

parts.name: Power supply 24 V 150 W, open frame

details.function: Turns mains power into 24 V for the board, the display and the fan.
details.why: Mounted low and at the back, next to the power inlet, to keep mains wiring short.

details.function: Pulls warm air out at the back of the device.
details.why: The arrow on the frame shows the airflow: it must point out of the device.
details.ifWrong: Fitted backwards it blows warm air into the device. It overheats only on hot days, so the mistake can go unnoticed for a long time.

details.function: Shows the user interface and reads the touch input.
details.why: Mounted on the front frame, not on the bezel, so the bezel can be changed without touching the display.

details.function: Carries the display and touch signals to the board (J3).
details.why: Flat cable is thin and flexible.
details.ifWrong: Fitted upside down or not fully inserted, the display shows nothing or flickers when warm.

parts.name: Protective earth wire, green/yellow, M4 ring terminal

details.function: Connects the earth pin of the power inlet to the chassis earth stud.
details.why: Green/yellow is the international colour for protective earth.

details.function: Holds the cables clear of the fan and of sharp edges.
details.why: Cheap, quick, and keeps the wiring the same in every device.

details.function: Stops small screws turning loose under vibration.
details.why: Low strength so the bezel can still be removed for service.
details.ifWrong: A high-strength (red) threadlocker would make the M3 screws break before they come out.

details.function: Identifies the device and its electrical rating.
details.why: Every device must carry its serial number so it can be traced.

details.function: A line of lacquer across nut and stud shows the joint was torqued and has not moved since.
details.why: An inspector can see at a glance whether a safety-critical joint is untouched.

details.function: Front and rear side of the base frame.
details.why: A 20 × 40 profile is stiff enough to keep the frame flat and square.

parts.name: Y rail, left, 2040 × 600 mm with belt

details.function: Left side of the frame. The gantry rolls along it.
details.ifWrong: Left and right rails are mirror images: swapped, the belts end up on the inside.

parts.name: Y rail, right, 2040 × 600 mm with belt

details.function: Right side of the frame. The gantry rolls along it.
details.ifWrong: Left and right rails are mirror images: swapped, the belts end up on the inside.

details.function: Carries the laser across the work area. Its two motors drive it front to back.
The blue diode laser that marks and cuts.
details.why: The orange shield blocks the scattered blue light toward the front.
details.ifWrong: A loose module makes blurred, doubled lines.

details.function: Drives the motors and the laser from the computer or the app.
Feeds the controller.
details.ifWrong: A 12 V adapter fits the same plug but the motors lose steps and the laser stays weak.

details.function: Holds the frame 26 mm above the table so the gantry wheels clear it.
Holds the end of a Y belt at the right tension.
Sets the distance between the laser and the material.
details.why: The beam is thinnest 8 mm below this module: in focus it marks finely, out of focus it only warms.

parts.name: Socket head cap screw M5 × 25, black
parts.tool: 4 mm hex key, torque driver at 3.5 N·m

details.function: Joins the rails to the front and rear profiles, into the tapped profile ends.
Feet and belt clamps, into slot nuts.
details.ifWrong: Mixed up with M5 × 10, it is 2 mm short and the controller box works loose.

details.function: Fixes the controller box, through its 2 mm mounting ears.
details.why: 10 mm = 2 mm ear + 3 mm slot wall + enough thread in the slot nut.

details.function: Clamps the laser module in its holder: hand tight, no tools.

parts.name: Slot nut M5 for 20 mm profile

details.function: Sits inside the profile slot so a screw can hold anything anywhere along it.

parts.name: Socket head cap screw M3 × 6, black

details.function: Holds each limit switch.
details.ifWrong: Over-tightened, it cracks the switch body.

details.function: Motors and limit switches to the controller.
Power and control for the laser module.
Tells the controller where the corner is, so every job starts from the same point.

devices.name: Nova-1 demo console
devices.description: A fictional bench-top console (power supply, control board, fan, touch display) made up to show how RightPart works. Its instructions contain one deliberate mistake for the integrity check to find.

steps.title: Fit the four board standoffs
steps.summary: Screw four 10 mm standoffs into the base plate where the main board will sit.
instructions: Place the chassis on the ESD mat with the front frame toward you.
Find the four holes marked B1–B4 on the right half of the base plate.
Screw a standoff into each hole by hand until it sits flat.
Tighten each standoff to 0.5 N·m.
checks: All four standoffs sit flat and upright
Earth stud is clean and undamaged

warnings.text: Brass is soft: above 0.6 N·m the thread can shear off in the base plate.

steps.why: The standoffs set the height of the main board. Every part fitted later lines up on them, so they must be fully seated.

steps.title: Mount the power supply
steps.summary: Fix the power supply to the left rear of the base plate with four Torx screws.
instructions: Check that the power supply label reads 24 V.
Set it on the left rear of the base plate, output terminals toward the board.
Fit the four screws through the flanges.
Tighten to 0.6 N·m in a cross pattern.
checks: Output terminals face the board
Flanges sit flat, no gap underneath
steps.why: The power supply is the heaviest part inside. Four tight screws stop it moving if the device is dropped.

steps.title: Fit the main board
steps.summary: Lower the board onto the standoffs and fix it with four screws and nylon washers.
instructions: Put on the ESD wrist strap and check it on the tester.
Hold the board by its edges, connectors toward the front.
Lower it onto the four standoffs.
Put a nylon washer under each screw and start all four screws by hand.
Tighten to 0.4 N·m in a cross pattern.
checks: The board does not rock
No scratches around the mounting holes

warnings.text: Static-sensitive: never touch the board without a grounded wrist strap.

steps.why: Tightening in a cross pattern pulls the board down evenly. Tightening one corner fully first can bend the board and crack solder joints.

steps.title: Fit the cooling fan
steps.summary: Fix the fan inside the rear wall with four long screws and new lock nuts.
instructions: Find the airflow arrow on the fan frame.
Hold the fan against the inside of the rear wall, arrow pointing out of the device, cable at the bottom.
Push the four screws in from outside the rear wall.
Fit a new lock nut on each screw inside.
Tighten to 0.3 N·m. The fan frame is plastic: do not over-tighten.
checks: Airflow arrow points out of the device
At least two threads show past each lock nut
The fan spins freely by hand

warnings.text: Lock nuts are single-use. Never refit one that has been removed.

steps.why: A fan fitted backwards blows warm air into the device instead of out. It only overheats on hot days, so the mistake can go unnoticed.

steps.title: Connect the protective earth
steps.summary: Clamp the earth wire on the earth stud between two star washers.
instructions: Fit the first star washer on the earth stud.
Fit the ring terminal of the green/yellow wire.
Fit the second star washer.
Fit the M4 nut and tighten to 1.2 N·m.
Draw a line of torque seal across the nut and the stud.
checks: Order: star washer, ring terminal, star washer, nut
Torque seal line across nut and stud
Nothing else fixed on the earth stud

warnings.text: Safety-critical: this joint protects the user from electric shock if a fault occurs.

steps.why: In a fault, current must flow to earth through this joint instead of through the person touching the device. The star washers cut through the anodising so the joint stays well below the safety limit for the life of the device.

steps.title: Fit the display
steps.summary: Fix the display to the front frame with four M2.5 screws.
instructions: Leave the protective film on the screen until final inspection.
Feed the display cable through the slot in the front frame.
Place the display on the front frame, connector at the bottom.
Fit the four screws through the mounting ears.
checks: Display sits flat with even gaps
Cable not pinched in the slot
steps.why: The display is fixed to the front frame, not to the bezel, so the bezel can be changed later without touching the display.

steps.title: Fit the front bezel
steps.summary: Fit the bezel over the display and fix it with six button head screws.

parts.note: Threadlocker on the first two threads

instructions: Check the bezel window is clean.
Place the bezel over the display, lined up on the six bosses.
Put a drop of threadlocker on the first two threads of each screw.
Fit the six screws and tighten to 0.6 N·m, top and bottom alternately.
checks: The bezel sits flat, no gap at the corners
All six screw heads sit flat on the bezel
steps.why: The bezel protects the edge of the display and closes the front. It must be clamped firmly so it does not rattle.

steps.title: Connect the cables
steps.summary: Connect display, fan and power cables to the board and tie them clear of the fan.
instructions: Connect the display cable to J3: blue stiffener up, push it in straight, close the latch.
Connect the fan cable to J5.
Connect the power supply output to J1.
Tie the cables to the anchor points with four cable ties and cut the tails flush.
checks: All connector latches closed
Cables clear of the fan blades
Tie tails cut flush
steps.why: A half-seated connector can pass the first test and fail in use when the device warms up.

steps.title: Fit the top cover
steps.summary: Close the device with the top cover and six button head screws.
instructions: Check that no loose parts or cable tie tails are left inside.
Lower the cover straight down, its sides outside the base plate.
Fit the six screws: three at the front, three at the rear.
Tighten to 0.6 N·m.
checks: No cable trapped under the cover edge
The cover sits flat on both flanges
steps.why: The cover keeps fingers and dust out. Six screws spread the clamping evenly.

steps.title: Final inspection and rating label
steps.summary: Test the earth bond, apply the rating label and record the result.
instructions: Shake the device gently: nothing should rattle.
Measure the earth bond from the earth pin of the power inlet to the chassis.
Print the rating label with the serial number and stick it on the rear wall above the fan.
Record the serial number and the test result in the build record.
checks: Earth bond below 0.1 Ω
Label serial number matches the build record
No rattle when shaken

warnings.text: Do not power the device until the earth bond test has passed.

steps.why: The earth bond test proves the protective earth joint from step 5 works. The label makes the device traceable for its whole life.

changes.text: Power supply screws changed to Torx (100-0236).
Front bezel screws changed from 100-0234 (M3 × 10) to 100-0233 (M3 × 8): the 10 mm screw bottoms out in the 5 mm bezel bosses.

objects.label: Power supply output (part of the power supply)

devices.name: Lumen LX-1 laser engraver
devices.description: Fictional desktop laser engraver for the demo: aluminium frame, moving gantry, 10 W diode laser.

steps.title: Build the frame
steps.summary: Join the four profiles into a square frame.
instructions: Lay the two rails on the table, belts facing out.
Put the front and rear profiles between them.
Fit two screws through each rail end into each profile.
Tighten all eight to 3.5 N·m.
checks: The frame sits flat
Both diagonals measure the same
steps.why: A frame out of square makes every engraving slightly skewed.

steps.title: Fit the feet
steps.summary: One foot under each corner.
instructions: Slide a slot nut into the outer slot near each corner.
Hold a foot bracket on it and fit the screw.
Tighten to 2.5 N·m.
checks: The frame does not rock

steps.title: Put on the gantry
steps.summary: Lower the gantry onto the rails and check it rolls.
instructions: Hold the gantry by the beam with both hands.
Set the wheels on the rails from the rear.
Turn the eccentric nuts until the wheels grip but still roll.
checks: The gantry rolls freely end to end
No wobble when you push it sideways

warnings.text: Lift the gantry by the beam, never by the motors.

steps.title: Clamp the belts
steps.summary: Fix both belt ends on each rail.
instructions: Pull the belt end into the clamp.
Fit the clamp on the rail end and tighten the screw.
Do the same at all four ends.
checks: Press a belt in the middle: it gives a little and springs back
Both belts feel the same
steps.why: Loose belts draw wavy lines; over-tight belts wear the motors.

steps.title: Fit the limit switches
steps.summary: One switch on the beam, one on the left rail.
instructions: Fit one switch on the left end of the beam.
Fit the other on the left rail, near the rear.
Tighten gently: the switch body is plastic.
checks: Push the gantry to the rear-left corner: both switches click

steps.title: Mount the laser
steps.summary: Slide the laser module into its holder.
instructions: Slide the module down into the holder on the carriage.
Tighten the thumb screw by hand.
checks: The module cannot move in the holder

warnings.text: Laser light can blind in an instant. Wear the safety glasses whenever the machine has power.

steps.title: Fit the controller
steps.summary: Fix the controller box on the front profile.
instructions: Slide two slot nuts into the front slot, right side.
Hold the box against the profile.
Fit the two screws through its ears.
checks: The box sits tight against the frame
steps.why: M5 × 10 here, not M5 × 8: the ears are thicker than the foot brackets.

steps.title: Connect the cables
steps.summary: Motors, switches and laser to the controller.
instructions: Plug the harness into the controller.
Plug each motor and switch: every plug is labelled.
Plug the laser cable into the module.
Tie the cables to the beam.
checks: Every plug clicks home
Move the gantry by hand: no cable snags

warnings.text: Never plug or unplug anything while the power is on.

steps.title: Set the focus
steps.summary: Use the gauge to set the laser height.
instructions: Put the test card under the laser.
Loosen the focus knob.
Lower the module until the gauge just touches the card.
Tighten the knob and take the gauge away.
checks: The gauge slides out with a light touch

steps.title: Power on and test
steps.summary: Home the machine and burn a small test square.
instructions: Put on the safety glasses.
Connect the power adapter and switch on.
Press Home: the gantry goes to the rear-left corner.
Burn a 10 mm square at 10% power on the test card.
checks: Homing stops at both switches
The test square is sharp and dark

warnings.text: Wear laser safety glasses. Never leave the laser running unattended, and keep a fire extinguisher at hand.

memory.note: Example mix-ups for the fictional Nova-1, so the demo shows what the app learns at the bench. Not real events.

trails.note: Example floor trails for the fictional Nova-1, placed a number of days before today so the demo stays current. Not real events.
